title: Vector equations of lines
summary: A straight line is fixed by one point on it and one direction. The [[vector-equation-of-a-line|vector equation of a line]], $\boldsymbol{r} = \boldsymbol{a} + \lambda\boldsymbol{b}$, gives every point on it, one for each value of $\lambda$. Split into [[parametric-form|parametric form]], it gives each coordinate on its own, which is how you find where a path meets the ground, a wall or a given point.

goals.text: Write a vector equation of a line from a point and a direction, or from two points, in 2D and 3D.
Read the point, the direction and the parameter $\lambda$ in context, and test whether a point lies on a line.
Convert between $\boldsymbol{r} = \boldsymbol{a} + \lambda\boldsymbol{b}$ and parametric form, and use parametric form to find the point where a line meets a condition.

synonyms: does a point lie on a line

before.prompt: The points $\mathrm{A}(4, -2, 1)$ and $\mathrm{B}(1, 3, 5)$ are given. Find $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}$.
before.explain: $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}} = \begin{pmatrix}1 - 4\\3 - (-2)\\5 - 1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-3\\5\\4\end{pmatrix}$. Subtracting the other way round reverses the direction, and $\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\5\end{pmatrix}$ is the [[position-vector|position vector]] of B. Revise it in {{lesson:3.10}}.

before.hint: Square each component, add the squares, then take the square root.
Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other: every component is multiplied by the same number.
before.explain: $\begin{pmatrix}-4\\2\\-6\end{pmatrix} = -2\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$, so it is parallel (it points the opposite way). In $\begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\\6\end{pmatrix}$ only two components were doubled. Revise it in {{lesson:3.10}}.

sections.heading: The vector equation of a line

blocks.text: In {{lesson:2.1}} you fixed a line in 2D by a point and a gradient. A line in 3D has no single gradient, so you give its direction as a [[vector|vector]] instead. One point and one direction pin down exactly one line.

Picture standing at a point A on a straight path. You reach every other point on the path by walking some multiple of the path's direction, forwards or backwards. A [[vector-equation-of-a-line|vector equation]] says this in symbols.

blocks.statement: The line through the point with position vector $\boldsymbol{a}$, parallel to the non-zero vector $\boldsymbol{b}$, has vector equation $\boldsymbol{r} = \boldsymbol{a} + \lambda\boldsymbol{b}$, where $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
blocks.plain: Start at a known point, then add any multiple of the direction.

blocks.text: $\boldsymbol{a}$ is the [[position-vector|position vector]] $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{OA}}$ of a known point A on the line. $\boldsymbol{b}$ is a [[direction-vector|direction vector]]: any non-zero vector parallel to the line. $\boldsymbol{r}$ is the position vector of a general point on the line.

$\lambda$ (lambda) is the parameter, a real number. Each value of $\lambda$ gives one point: $\lambda = 0$ gives A, $\lambda = 1$ gives the point one step of $\boldsymbol{b}$ further on, and negative values go backwards. As $\lambda$ takes every real value, the points fill the whole line.
The formula is in the booklet. Always start with $\boldsymbol{r} =$. Without it you have an expression, not an equation. The same equation works in 2D, with two components, and in 3D, with three.
For a line through two points P and Q, start at either point. For the direction, use the displacement $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{PQ}} = \boldsymbol{q} - \boldsymbol{p}$.

blocks.alt: Axes with origin O. A straight cycle path runs from the cafe C at (-20, 50) down to the gate G at (60, -10), and a dashed line continues it beyond both ends. A vector a runs from O to C. A bold vector b runs along the path from C to G. Points on the line are marked lambda equals 0 at C, lambda equals 0.5 halfway along, and lambda equals 1 at G. A dashed vector r runs from O to the point where lambda equals 0.5.
blocks.caption: With $\boldsymbol{a} = \overrightarrow{\mathrm{OC}}$ and $\boldsymbol{b} = \overrightarrow{\mathrm{CG}}$, values $0 \le \lambda \le 1$ give the path itself. Here $\boldsymbol{r} = \boldsymbol{a} + 0.5\boldsymbol{b}$ is its midpoint.

blocks.question: A park is mapped with its entrance at the origin O, $x$ metres east and $y$ metres north. A straight cycle path runs from a café at $\mathrm{C}(-20, 50)$ to a gate at $\mathrm{G}(60, -10)$. Find a vector equation of the line along the path, starting at C. Find and interpret the point given by $\lambda = 0.25$.
steps: $\lambda = 0.25$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}-20 + 0.25(80)\\50 + 0.25(-60)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\35\end{pmatrix}$: the point $(0, 35)$, 35 m due north of the entrance.

Interpret: the path is $\lvert\overrightarrow{\mathrm{CG}}\rvert = \sqrt{80^{2} + (-60)^{2}} = 100$ m long, so this point is a quarter of the way along, 25 m from the café. Values of $\lambda$ outside $0 \le \lambda \le 1$ give points on the line beyond the ends of the path.

blocks.question: A ski lift's cable runs in a straight line from the bottom station $\mathrm{B}(120, 40, 15)$ to the top station $\mathrm{T}(-80, 290, 515)$. Coordinates are in metres: $x$ east, $y$ north and $z$ height above a reference level. (a) Write down a vector equation of the cable's line in the form $\boldsymbol{r} = \overrightarrow{\mathrm{OB}} + \lambda\overrightarrow{\mathrm{BT}}$. (b) The top of a support tower is at $(40, 140, 215)$. Show that it lies on the line, find the value of $\lambda$ there and interpret it.
steps: (b) Set the general point equal to the tower top. From $x$: $120 - 200\lambda = 40$, so $\lambda = 0.4$.
Check the other components with $\lambda = 0.4$: $y = 40 + 250(0.4) = 140$ and $z = 15 + 500(0.4) = 215$. One value of $\lambda$ gives all three coordinates, so the tower top lies on the line.
Interpret: $\lambda = 0$ is B and $\lambda = 1$ is T, so the tower top is $40\%$ of the way along the cable from the bottom station.

blocks.text: Testing a point with one component only. Any single equation gives some $\lambda$. The point is on the line only if the same $\lambda$ works in every component.

A line has many vector equations. You can start at any point on it, and any non-zero multiple of $\boldsymbol{b}$ is also a direction vector. Above, $\begin{pmatrix}-200\\250\\500\end{pmatrix} = 50\begin{pmatrix}-4\\5\\10\end{pmatrix}$, so $\begin{pmatrix}-4\\5\\10\end{pmatrix}$ gives the same line.

The meaning of $\lambda$ changes with the equation, though. With direction $\begin{pmatrix}-4\\5\\10\end{pmatrix}$, $\lambda = 1$ is no longer the top station. So read $\lambda$ from the equation you were given.

In 2D, the line $y = mx + c$ passes through $(0, c)$ and rises $m$ for every $1$ across. So $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\c\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\m\end{pmatrix}$ is a vector equation of it. Going back, a direction $\begin{pmatrix}p\\q\end{pmatrix}$ with $p \ne 0$ gives the gradient $\frac{q}{p}$.

blocks.prompt: Which is a vector equation of the line through $\mathrm{P}(3, -1, 2)$ and $\mathrm{Q}(5, 2, -2)$?
blocks.hint: The direction is $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{PQ}}$: subtract the coordinates of P from those of Q.
blocks.explain: $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{PQ}} = \begin{pmatrix}5 - 3\\2 - (-1)\\-2 - 2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-4\end{pmatrix}$. Using $\begin{pmatrix}5\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ treats Q's position vector as a direction, and the last option swaps the point and the direction.

blocks.prompt: Which is a vector equation of the line $y = 3x - 2$?
blocks.hint: Find one point on the line, such as where $x = 0$. Then move $1$ across: how far up do you go?
blocks.explain: $x = 0$ gives $y = -2$, so $(0, -2)$ is on the line. A gradient of $3$ means $3$ up for $1$ across, so the direction is $\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\end{pmatrix}$. The point $(-2, 0)$ is not on the line: $3(-2) - 2 = -8$.

blocks.text: A [[vector-equation-of-a-line|vector equation]] holds two or three equations in one. Write $\boldsymbol{r}$ as $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}$, the known point as $(x_{0}, y_{0}, z_{0})$ and the direction as $\begin{pmatrix}l\\m\\n\end{pmatrix}$. Then each row gives one coordinate.

blocks.tex: x = x_{0} + \lambda l, \quad y = y_{0} + \lambda m, \quad z = z_{0} + \lambda n

blocks.text: This is the [[parametric-form|parametric form]] of the line, and it is in the booklet too. Each coordinate is written in terms of the parameter $\lambda$. In 2D you have only the $x$ and $y$ equations.

Parametric form is how you use a line. A condition such as “on the ground” ($z = 0$) or “at the wall $x = 5$” gives one equation in $\lambda$. Solve it, then put that $\lambda$ into every coordinate. If that coordinate has no $\lambda$ term, the line is parallel to the ground or wall: it never meets it, or lies in it.

blocks.question: Relative to a depot O, a delivery drone descends along the line $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}12\\-5\\60\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\\-15\end{pmatrix}$. Distances are in metres: $x$ east, $y$ north and $z$ height above flat ground. Write the line in parametric form, and find the coordinates of the point where the drone lands.
steps: Substitute $\lambda = 4$ into the other two: $x = 12 + 4(4) = 28$ and $y = -5 + 3(4) = 7$.
Interpret: the drone lands 28 m east and 7 m north of the depot, assuming it keeps to the straight line until it touches down.

blocks.text: Answering in the wrong form. When a question asks for coordinates, write $(28, 7, 0)$. Some mark schemes condone a column vector, but give one only when a position vector is asked for.

Going back from parametric to vector form is reading off. The constants give the point and the coefficients of $\lambda$ give the direction. A coordinate with no $\lambda$ term has direction component $0$.

blocks.question: A zip line is modelled by $x = 25 - 8\lambda$, $y = 12 + 6\lambda$, $z = 30 - 5\lambda$, where distances are in metres and $z$ is the height above the ground. A rider starts at $\lambda = 0$. (a) Write down a vector equation of the zip line. (b) The zip line ends at a landing platform where $x = -15$. Find the length of the zip line. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
steps: (a) Constants give the start, coefficients of $\lambda$ give the direction: $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}25\\12\\30\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}-8\\6\\-5\end{pmatrix}$.
(b) At the landing platform, $25 - 8\lambda = -15$, so $\lambda = 5$. The end point is $(25 - 8(5), 12 + 6(5), 30 - 5(5)) = (-15, 42, 5)$.
Displacement from start to end: $\begin{pmatrix}-15 - 25\\42 - 12\\5 - 30\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-40\\30\\-25\end{pmatrix}$. That is $5$ times the direction vector, as $\lambda = 5$ says.
Write down what you enter: length $= \left\lvert\begin{pmatrix}-40\\30\\-25\end{pmatrix}\right\rvert = \sqrt{(-40)^{2} + 30^{2} + (-25)^{2}} = 55.9016\ldots$ m.

Interpret: each unit of $\lambda$ moves $\sqrt{125} = 11.18\ldots$ m along the line, and the rider travels $5$ units. The end is still $5$ m above the ground, a sensible height for a landing platform.

blocks.text: On Paper 2, write the vector or expression you put into the GDC before its value. That line earns the method mark even if the final figure slips.

blocks.prompt: The point $(7, k, 26)$ lies on the line $x = -1 + 2\lambda$, $y = 4 - 3\lambda$, $z = 6 + 5\lambda$. Find $k$.
blocks.hint: Use a coordinate without $k$ to find $\lambda$. Check it in the other one.

blocks.prompt: A line has parametric form $x = 1 - 4\lambda$, $y = 6$, $z = 3 + 2\lambda$. Which is a vector equation of the line?
blocks.hint: Collect the constants into the point and the coefficients of $\lambda$ into the direction. What is the coefficient of $\lambda$ in $y = 6$?
blocks.explain: The constants $1$, $6$ and $3$ give the point. The coefficients of $\lambda$ are $-4$, $0$ and $2$: $y$ stays at $6$, so the line never moves in the $y$-direction. The sign of $-4\lambda$ belongs in the direction.

blocks.text: In $\boldsymbol{r} = \boldsymbol{a} + \lambda\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{a}$ is the position vector of any point on the line and $\boldsymbol{b}$ is any non-zero vector parallel to it. Through P and Q, use $\boldsymbol{b} = \overrightarrow{\mathrm{PQ}} = \boldsymbol{q} - \boldsymbol{p}$.

For $\boldsymbol{r} = \overrightarrow{\mathrm{OP}} + \lambda\overrightarrow{\mathrm{PQ}}$: $\lambda = 0$ is P, $\lambda = 1$ is Q, and $0 \le \lambda \le 1$ is the segment PQ. With a different point or direction, $\lambda$ means something different.
A point lies on a line only if one value of $\lambda$ gives every one of its coordinates.

blocks.tex: x = x_{0} + \lambda l, \quad y = y_{0} + \lambda m, \quad z = z_{0} + \lambda n

blocks.text: From parametric form back to $\boldsymbol{r} = \boldsymbol{a} + \lambda\boldsymbol{b}$: the constants give the point, the coefficients of $\lambda$ give the direction, and a coordinate with no $\lambda$ term has direction component $0$.

To find where a line meets a condition such as $z = 0$: solve that coordinate's equation for $\lambda$, then substitute that $\lambda$ into every coordinate. If that coordinate has no $\lambda$ term, there is no single meeting point.

mistakes: Leaving out $\boldsymbol{r} =$. On its own, $\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\end{pmatrix}$ is an expression, not an equation, and can lose a mark.
Using a position vector as the direction. For the line through P and Q, the direction is $\boldsymbol{q} - \boldsymbol{p}$, not $\boldsymbol{q}$.
Testing a point with one coordinate only. Find $\lambda$ from one coordinate, then show that the same $\lambda$ gives the others too.
Mixing up the parts of parametric form: putting a constant into the direction, or forgetting that a coordinate with no $\lambda$ term has direction component $0$.
Rounding $\lambda$ before substituting it. Keep the full value and round only the final coordinates or length.
examTips: “Write down” a vector equation: no working is needed, but give the whole equation, starting $\boldsymbol{r} =$. The point and the direction vector can earn separate marks.
“Show that” a point lies on a line: find $\lambda$ from one coordinate, substitute it into the others, and state the conclusion. The reasoning mark needs evidence that every coordinate agrees.

“Find the coordinates” of a point on a line: write the equation you solve for $\lambda$, such as $60 - 15\lambda = 0$, then substitute. Give coordinates, not a column vector, unless a position vector is asked for.
“Interpret” $\lambda$ in context: say which points $\lambda = 0$ and $\lambda = 1$ are. In {{lesson:3.12}} the parameter is time and the direction vector is a velocity.
